issues.legal_issue: The statutory time limits and consequences of default in the general land-acquisition law do not apply to an acquisition carried out under a self-contained planned-development statute when importing them would undermine that statute’s scheme.
material_facts: The appeal concerned land included in an acquisition initiated for a development scheme under a state development statute.
The appellant argued that the acquisition had lapsed because the award was made beyond the period prescribed by the general land-acquisition law.
The state statute provided its own scheme for planned development, specified when a scheme would lapse, and applied the general land-acquisition law only so far as its provisions were applicable.
The Court found that importing the general law’s acquisition deadlines and consequences of default could frustrate the planned-development scheme.
issues.conclusion: The general law’s time limits and consequences of default, including the provision for lapse of acquisition, cannot be read into acquisitions under the state development statute; the general law’s provision requiring an award within a specified period therefore does not apply.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 27 and 36 of the Bangalore Development Authority Act, the state statute provides a self-contained scheme and applies the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 only so far as its provisions are applicable. Provisions concerning acquisition, compensation and legal remedies may apply where the state statute has no corresponding provisions, but its own scheme and consequences of default exclude incompatible deadlines and lapse provisions such as Section 11A. This approach follows Land Acquisition Officer, City Improvement Trust Board v. H. Narayanaiah, Munithimmaiah v. State of Karnataka and Bondu Ramaswamy v. Bangalore Development Authority, and is consistent with Girnar Traders III.

predicates.acquisition_for_planned_development: The public authority undertook the acquisition as part of a statutory planned-development scheme.
predicates.state_statute_has_its_own_scheme_and_def: The state development statute sets out its own scheme and specifies consequences for failure to carry it out.
predicates.imported_deadline_would_frustrate_the_sc: Applying a deadline from the general acquisition law would undermine or frustrate the state development scheme.

issues.definition: When an acquisition is for planned development, the state statute supplies its own scheme and consequences of default, and importing an outside deadline would frustrate that scheme, the general acquisition deadline does not apply.

issues.legal_issue: A state law whose predominant purpose is planned development may incidentally provide for land acquisition without being invalid merely because acquisition is also addressed by central legislation, if the laws can operate without irreconcilable conflict.
material_facts: The state statute established a development authority and provided for the formulation and implementation of planned-development schemes.
Land acquisition under that statute was incidental to the schemes’ development purpose.

The appellant contended that acquisition was governed by the concurrent legislative field and that the state statute conflicted with the central land-acquisition law; the state statute had not received presidential assent.
The Court concluded that the state statute was principally concerned with planned development, fell within the state legislative field, and could coexist with the central law.
issues.conclusion: The state development statute is within the State Legislature’s competence and is not invalid on grounds of repugnancy with the central land-acquisition law.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 246 and 254 of the Constitution, read with Entries 5 and 18 of List II and Entry 42 of List III, permit the State Legislature to enact a law principally concerned with local authorities, land and planned development, even if acquisition is an incident of that law. Applying the doctrines of pith and substance, incidental encroachment and harmonious construction, repugnancy requires an actual, irreconcilable conflict; incidental overlap does not suffice. The Court relied on Munithimmaiah v. State of Karnataka, Bondu Ramaswamy v. Bangalore Development Authority, A.S. Krishna v. Madras State, State of West Bengal v. Kesoram Industries Ltd. and Girnar Traders III.

predicates.state_law_for_planned_development: The challenged state law principally establishes a public authority or scheme for planned development.
predicates.acquisition_is_incidental: The law provides for acquisition as an incident of achieving its planned-development purpose rather than making acquisition its primary object.
predicates.laws_can_operate_without_irreconcilable_: The state law and the central law can operate in their respective fields without an actual, irreconcilable conflict.

issues.definition: When a state law principally serves planned development, acquisition is incidental to that purpose, and the laws can operate without irreconcilable conflict, the state development law is not invalid for repugnancy.

issues.legal_issue: The lapse of a development scheme does not reverse the vesting of land that has already been acquired and vested in the State or the development authority.
material_facts: The Court considered the relationship between lapse of a development scheme and the status of land acquired under it.
It explained that land acquired and vested in the State, and subsequently transferred to the development authority, is vested free from encumbrances.
The state statute contained no provision automatically revesting such land in its former owner upon lapse of the scheme.
issues.conclusion: If acquisition has been completed and the land has vested in the State, lapse of the development scheme does not cause the acquisition to lapse or restore title to the former owner.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 27 and 36(3) of the Bangalore Development Authority Act distinguish lapse of a scheme from the status of completed acquisition; Section 16 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 provides for vesting upon completion of acquisition. Once land has vested free from encumbrances, lapse of the scheme does not reverse title absent a statutory mechanism for revesting, such as the one contemplated by Section 37(3) of the Bangalore Development Authority Act. If acquisition is still pending and vesting has not occurred, the effect of scheme lapse depends on the circumstances and the statutory scheme.

predicates.development_scheme_has_lapsed: The statutory development scheme has lapsed.
predicates.acquisition_was_completed: The compulsory acquisition proceedings were completed before the scheme lapsed.
predicates.land_has_vested_in_public_authority: The land vested in the State or was transferred to the public development authority.

issues.definition: When a development scheme has lapsed after acquisition was completed and the land vested in a public authority, the acquisition title is not reverted.
